The Chartered Institute of Stockbrokers (CIS) has launched a N5 billion Endowment Fund to promote research, professional education and human capital development in Nigeria’s capital market.
The launch was a major highlight of the Institute’s 30th Annual Conference, held in Lagos, with the theme, ‘From Capital Mobilised to Prosperity Realised: Financing Nigeria’s Next Era of Growth and Global Competitiveness’.
Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, endorsed the fund and pledged the state government’s support.
Sanwo-Olu, himself a stockbroker, disclosed that Lagos State had raised more than N200 billion through the capital market to finance infrastructure development.
He said the experience showed what was possible when the market was used productively, and why sustained investment in people and knowledge was critical.
The endowment fund is expected to support capital market research, scholarships, the establishment of a professorial chair, academic excellence and professional capacity development.
President of CIS, Dr Fiona Ahimie, said the fund was part of a deliberate effort to ensure that market growth is matched by professional depth.
She said the success of the capital market should be measured not only by market capitalisation, transaction volumes and funds raised, but also by its contributions to infrastructure development, industrial growth, employment generation and improved living standards.
Ahimie described the market as a critical bridge between savings and businesses requiring long-term financing, stressing that capital mobilisation must translate into productive investments capable of generating sustainable economic growth.
The director-general of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Dr Emomotimi Agama, said technology was transforming capital raising and trading.
He disclosed that the Commission was deploying sophisticated solutions to strengthen surveillance, enhance oversight and detect market abuses to protect investors and sustain confidence.
The director-general of the National Pension Commission (PenCom), Omolola Oloworaran, identified pension assets as a major source of long-term capital, but stressed that investments must be guided by prudence and protection of contributors’ savings.
The director-general of the Debt Management Office (DMO), Patience Oniha, advocated deeper participation in the domestic bond market and deployment of debt capital productively to finance infrastructure.
Chairman of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), Otunba Francis Meshioye, argued that Nigeria’s challenge was not merely availability of capital but limited channels to productive enterprises.
To address the estimated $2.3 trillion infrastructure deficit, he advocated pension funds, infrastructure bonds, green bonds, Sukuk and public-private partnerships.
Also, Group chairman of Nigerian Exchange Group, Alhaji Umaru Kwairanga, challenged stockbrokers to move beyond transaction execution and become facilitators of economic development.
The chief executive officer of Chapel Hill Denham, Bolaji Balogun, acknowledged gains from reforms including the Investments and Securities Act 2025, the shift from T+3 to T+2 and then T+1 settlement, and extended trading hours.
He cautioned, however, that improved infrastructure would not automatically produce a deeper market, calling for more quality listings, wider investor participation and innovative instruments, including project bonds, infrastructure funds, Sukuk, green and orange bonds, and convertible securities.
